title: Job 8:1–7
context: Job 8:1–7 opens the first speech of Bildad the Shuhite, the speaker throughout chapter 8, who answers Job’s laments in chapters 6–7. Bildad asks how long Job’s words will be “a mighty wind” (8:2) and asks, “Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?” (8:3). He supposes, “If your children have sinned against him”, that they were handed over to their disobedience (8:4; compare 1:5, 1:18–19), and he urges Job to seek God, promising that “If you were pure and upright”, God would restore him (8:5–7). These are a friend’s words, not the book’s verdict. The narrator has already introduced Job with the words “That man was blameless and upright” (1:1), the LORD speaks of him in the same way (1:8; 2:3), and the reader knows from the opening scenes what Bildad does not. The book’s own word about the three friends comes later, at 42:7, and these notes leave it to do its work there. Bildad is not wrong that God does not pervert justice (compare Deuteronomy 32:4), and both traditions treat that conviction as shared ground; the question the book presses is whether Job’s suffering proves Job’s guilt, which Bildad assumes and the prologue does not support.

verses.arminianNotes: Bildad the Shuhite now takes his turn, the second of the three friends to speak after Eliphaz. Arminian readers note that the friends came to comfort Job (2:11), and they read Bildad’s speech as a sincere but misdirected attempt to defend God’s justice in front of a suffering man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bildad answers Job directly, so his speech must be read as part of a dialogue rather than as a free-standing statement of doctrine. They hold that the book places his words under the later judgment of the LORD, without assuming every line is false.

verses.text: “How long will you speak these things? Shall the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad opens by calling Job’s words a mighty wind, that is, loud but empty. Arminian readers see here a friend who has stopped listening, and they note how quickly a defense of God can turn into impatience with the anguish of someone who is hurting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bildad treats Job’s laments as an offense against God’s honor, and they see a warning in his tone: zeal for God’s name does not excuse dismissing a sufferer whose situation the speaker does not understand, as the prologue shows.

verses.text: Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad asks, “Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?” Arminian readers affirm the answer he expects, that God never perverts justice, and they note that the error lies not in this conviction but in assuming that Job’s suffering must be the result of his own wrongdoing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that the Judge of all does right (compare Deuteronomy 32:4), and they treat the question as shared ground. They add that Bildad turns a true confession about God into a tight rule for reading every event, which the book will not allow.

verses.text: If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their disobedience.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad says, “If your children have sinned against him”, they were delivered into the hand of their disobedience. Arminian readers find this conditional painfully harsh toward a father who had offered sacrifices for his children (1:5), and they note that the prologue gives no such cause for their deaths (1:18–19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bildad reasons from the outcome back to a hidden sin, an assumption the reader knows to be unfounded. They read the line as a friend’s charge, not the book’s verdict, and they see it as a caution against explaining particular deaths as particular judgments.

verses.text: If you want to seek God diligently, make your supplication to the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad urges Job to seek God diligently and make supplication to the Almighty. Arminian readers agree that seeking God in prayer is right in every circumstance, and they note that Job does keep turning to God, though in lament and complaint rather than in the repentance Bildad has in mind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that supplication to God is always fitting and that God hears his people. They observe, however, that Bildad’s counsel presumes Job has something specific to confess, so a good exhortation is framed by a mistaken diagnosis of Job’s condition.

verses.text: If you were pure and upright, surely now he would awaken for you, and make the habitation of your righteousness prosperous.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad promises, “If you were pure and upright, surely now he would awaken for you”. Arminian readers note the irony that the narrator has already called Job “blameless and upright” (1:1), and they see Bildad’s conditional as a friend’s charge that quietly implies Job is neither pure nor upright.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bildad makes Job’s restoration depend directly on proving his purity, so that present prosperity becomes the visible sign of righteousness. They read this as a friend’s charge, not the book’s verdict, and they leave the later verdict at 42:7 to do its own work.

verses.text: Though your beginning was small, yet your latter end would greatly increase.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad pictures a small beginning and a greatly increased latter end. Arminian readers note that the book does end with Job’s latter days blessed (42:10), but they observe that this comes through the LORD’s own dealing with Job and not as a reward for following Bildad’s advice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same irony and add that God’s eventual blessing of Job is his free act after he has spoken from the whirlwind, not the outworking of a formula. They hold that God may bless or withhold in this life for purposes he has not disclosed.
